transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-07-21
Time: 15:00 PDT
Duration: ~45 mins
Recording link: https://app.fireflies.ai/recording/ff-20250721-9843
Attendees: Ava (Redwood AE), Noah (Redwood SE), Marta (CSM), Ethan (Infra), Priya (BlueLeaf ML), Marcus (BlueLeaf Platform), Sofia (Head of AI), Timothy (SRE)

Auto-summary: quick sync on pilot TTFT and streaming behavior on edge-like instances; discussed kernel choices, sequence length variance, intermittent perf regressions when sequence > 1024, and a noisy upstream load pattern. Agreed to run full kernel matrix and share results; customer to provide prompt traces and logs.

Topics: TTFT variability, streaming vs batch tradeoffs, KV cache warmup, kernel selection heuristics, quantization artifacts, observability/trace collection.

[00:00] Ava: hey everybody thanks for joining um we'll do a quick 45 minute check in, go over the bench numbers from last night and then action items.
[00:12] Priya: great thanks, short on time today so we'll try to be tight.
[00:18] Noah: cool i pulled the traces from the 03:00 run — there are two things to call out: first TTFT spikes at cold starts up to ~420ms; second streaming latency per token is fine but we see variance when sequence length jumps beyond 900 tokens.
[00:28] Marcus: yep we saw that too; the workload is very bursty sometimes a single request with 2k tokens shows up which blows up the batcher.
[00:35] Ethan: to confirm, these are edge-ish instances (A100 small) with local nvme cache, right?
[00:40] Priya: correct, we're trying to emulate a regional edge pool — smaller gpu and less mem. memory pressure's definitely a factor.
[00:50] Noah: right -- our hypothesis: two orthogonal causes. kernel selection falls back to the generic matmul kernel at certain sequence lengths; that increases kernel launch overhead. and second, KV cache warmup on cold requests causes the TTFT spike. will explain with numbers.
[01:05] Sofia: sorry quick Q — when you say kernel fallback is that the same as the 'evm' fallback we saw in the docs?
[01:12] Noah: yes but the doc name is matmul/gemm fallback — evm is an older internal name, docs sometimes mismatch. the short: the runtime picks an alternate path if it estimates perf will be worse for specific dims. sometimes the heuristics misfire for our workload.
[01:25] Priya: ok interesting, we do have a bimodal sequence distribution — many short prompts ~120 tokens and occasional long ones ~2k.
[01:32] Noah: that causes two things: (1) the batcher keeps waiting for longer requests and that increases latency for short ones; (2) when a long request comes, the kernel choice differs and the device occupancy pattern shifts, causing extra padding/compilation in hot paths.
[01:48] Ava: can you walk through the bench numbers from last night Noah?
[01:52] Noah: sure, so i ran three variants: baseline (no quant), q4f16 quant profile, and a tuned kernel set where we force a smaller-gemm path up to 1024 seq and fallback afterwards. Baseline median TTFT: 210ms, P95 390ms. Quant run median TTFT 170ms, P95 360ms but we saw more jitter in streaming. Tuned kernel median TTFT 160ms, P95 310ms but with a regression for sequences >1200 where P99 spiked to 1.2s.
[02:20] Timothy: that P99 is concerning — is it an I/O issue or compute scheduling?
[02:24] Noah: looks compute-bound — kernel compilation and some kernel launch overhead. there's also an interplay with the prefix cache invalidation at ~1k tokens.
[02:33] Marcus: prefix cache invalidation — is that the KV cache hit-rate dropping?
[02:36] Noah: yes, when the sequence length crosses our cache shard threshold we evict and recompute states, which adds ~80-200ms depending on context size.
[02:45] Priya: hmm we can't afford frequent evictions, our app keeps context for a whole session and this will break UX.
[02:50] Ava: right — so options: raise cache shard limits (memory cost), change rollout to favor smaller max seq on the edge, or do dynamic batching heuristics to isolate long requests.
[03:05] Sofia: any quick wins we can apply before the bench run?
[03:08] Noah: a quick win is to force a consistent kernel path by patching the heuristic — i can push a runtime flag to your env that forces the optimized small-seq kernel up to 1536 tokens. that reduces kernel switching overhead at the cost of some compute efficiency on truly large sequences.
[03:22] Priya: would that regress throughput for the 2k requests?
[03:24] Noah: minimal for low QPS of long requests; worst-case we see 5-10% throughput hit on large-single-request bursts but TTFT for short ones improves significantly.
[03:34] Marcus: what's the impact on token cost? our cost model is tight.
[03:37] Noah: on our run quant + kernel-fix reduced tokens/sec cost by ~12% overall due to better packing and fewer retries, but if you calibrate for extreme 2k loads you might pay ~6% more into those specific runs.
[03:48] Ava: Marta, any customer engagement notes?
[03:51] Marta: Priya wants to see an end-to-end bench with their prompt sets and also wants the security checklist before we kick a dedicated pilot.
[03:58] Priya: yes can you also include trace-level logs? we need to see the per-token timing.
[04:03] Noah: that's the plan — we'll collect perf traces (kernel timings, device occupancy, batch composition) and attach to the benchmark sheet. I'm going to annotate the rows where fallback occurs.
[04:12] Priya: also curious about streaming chunks — sometimes the client sees uneven token bursts — is that on the server chunking logic?
[04:18] Noah: could be either; by default we flush every N tokens but also wait for batch alignment. in bursts the flush timing can be delayed. we can change flush-to-client policy to be stricter (lower N) to smooth UX but that increases RPC overhead.
[04:31] Timothy: what's the recommended flush size for edge? our network rtt is ~60ms typical.
[04:35] Ethan: with 60ms RTT we recommend flush sizes that ensure token latency < 60ms; in practice that's 8-12 tokens depending on model. but if you lower tokens per flush you'll increase per-token cost by ~3-7%.
[04:49] Priya: tradeoffs understood. for our product UX we prefer slightly higher cost but smoother streaming.
[04:54] Noah: ok we'll add a bench variation with flush size 8 and quant+kernel fix.
[05:00] Ava: any security/compliance asks?
[05:03] Sofia: we need the SOC2 checklist and encryption-at-rest details; if we move to dedicated pool we need KMS integration.
[05:09] Marta: acknowledged — i'll send the Security one-pager and the dedicated deployment checklist after call.
[05:14] Ava: great. quick question — did we try model-slicing (hot model shards) to keep small-seq paths resident?
[05:20] Noah: not yet in this pilot, that's more of a Dedicated optimization but we can prototype a hot-slice pin for sessions which would help TTFT dramatically. I'll add as an investigatory task.
[05:30] Priya: ok timeline: we'd like to decide on dedicated vs hosted by end of month — if dedicated, we need perf SLAs and security docs.
[05:37] Ava: understood. we'll prioritize the kernel matrix and security checklist to meet that cadence.
[05:42] Marta: next steps recap: Redwood runs kernel matrix and annotated traces; BlueLeaf uploads prompts/logs; schedule bench review 07/28.
[05:50] Priya: perfect.
[05:52] (crosstalk)
[05:55] Ava: thanks everyone, end time 15:45 PDT.

References mentioned: benchmark spreadsheet (internal link: /s/blueleaf-pilot-bench), security one-pager, runtime flag patch (noah/runtime/force-smallseq-flag).

End transcript.
